## Last time: design the evaluation before fitting {.smaller}

In Lecture A, we:

- defined one prediction and the cases the conclusion should describe;
- separated the **signal check** from the **model-upgrade check**;
- chose accuracy and average recall for different statistical purposes;
- treated the data split as a choice about the future distribution;
- used paired comparisons because both methods predict the same requests;
- recorded these decisions in a design brief.

Today we use EDA and a plausible analysis plan to see whether those decisions
survive contact with the data.

## Start with the claim, not the code {.smaller}

Our help-desk question from Lecture A was:

> For later email requests in four queues, how much more often does a language
> model predict the recorded queue than a simple word model?

That one sentence fixes several choices:

- one prediction is made for one email request;
- the target is the recorded queue;
- the cases of interest arrive later;
- the complex model is compared with the simple model;
- the result is a difference in accuracy.

## A plausible AI-generated plan {.smaller}

> Randomly split all available requests. Remove rare words using the full
> file. Try several queue groupings and model settings. Report the setup with
> the highest test accuracy and use the language model if it wins.

Nothing here looks absurd. That is why it needs an audit.

Before discussing code, underline every phrase that quietly makes a study
decision.

## Use EDA to follow the study from data to claim {.smaller .compact-table}

| Stage | What EDA should make visible |
|---|---|
| Cases | who entered the file—and who did not |
| Outcome | how queue labels were produced and how common they are |
| Structure | time order, repeated people, templates, and near-duplicates |
| Features | vocabulary, missing text, and changes in wording |
| Evaluation | which cases, metrics, and comparisons answer the question |
| Claim | which future requests the result can reasonably describe |

EDA exposes mismatches early. A later modeling step cannot make email-only
data represent phone calls.

## Use three plain questions for every weak choice {.smaller}

| Question | Example answer |
|---|---|
| What could go wrong? | Similar requests may appear in training and test. |
| Why does that matter here? | The test should represent later, genuinely new requests. |
| How would we change it? | Split by time and check repeated groups. |

Avoid stopping at a label such as “bias” or “leakage.” State the path from the
choice to the misleading result.

::: notes
[Further reading] This follows the Cochrane Handbook's risk-of-bias framework:
ask structured questions, judge how a design choice could affect the result,
and justify the response.
https://training.cochrane.org/handbook/current/chapter-08
:::

## One split can answer the wrong question {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.7
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 3.7), sharex=True)
years = np.array([2022, 2023, 2024, 2025])

axes[0].scatter([2022, 2023, 2024, 2025], [1, 1, 1, 1],
                s=240, c=["#155a8a", "#c41230", "#155a8a", "#c41230"])
axes[0].set_title("Random rows: every year contributes to both sides")
axes[0].text(2025.1, 1, " training / test mixed", va="center", fontsize=10)

axes[1].scatter([2022, 2023, 2024], [1, 1, 1], s=240, color="#155a8a")
axes[1].scatter([2025], [1], s=240, color="#c41230")
axes[1].set_title("Time split: earlier requests train; later requests test")
axes[1].text(2025.1, 1, " test", va="center", fontsize=10)

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_ylim(.75, 1.25)
    ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
axes[1].set_xticks(years)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

If the claim is about later requests, the time split rehearses that future use.

## Time order and repeated groups are separate checks {.smaller}

Suppose one template appears in both 2023 and 2025. A time split respects the
calendar but still lets closely related text cross the boundary.

```python
shared = set(training["similarity_group"]) & set(test["similarity_group"])
print("groups in both sets:", len(shared))
assert len(shared) == 0
```

The code makes the rule checkable. It does not explain why the rule is right;
that explanation comes from the intended use.

## Why repeated groups can make a test look easier {.smaller}

Imagine each customer group uses a distinctive signature:

| Group | Training request | Test request |
|---|---|---|
| 17 | “acct-reset-17 password failed” | “acct-reset-17 login failed” |
| 42 | “vpn-device-42 cannot connect” | “vpn-device-42 offline” |

With a random-row split, the model can learn the group fingerprint and see it
again at test time. A group-held-out split removes that shortcut.

This is **duplicate contamination**: closely related cases cross the split and
make the test less like genuinely new cases.

## A small simulation makes the shortcut visible {.smaller}

Imagine simulated data with repeated requests from the same customer groups.
Each group uses a stable identifying phrase, and that phrase partly predicts
its queue. The two test designs represent different future settings:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
results = {"Random rows\n(groups overlap)": 0.91,
           "Groups held out\n(no overlap)": 0.64}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.2))
bars = ax.bar(results.keys(), results.values(), color=["#c41230", "#155a8a"])
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("test accuracy")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
for bar, value in zip(bars, results.values()):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2, value + .025,
            f"{value:.2f}", ha="center")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

These are illustrative results, not a universal law. If future requests come
from the **same customer groups**, random rows may be the better representation
of future use. If the model must serve **new groups**, holding out groups is the
relevant test. Neither split is inherently more valid; each targets a different
future distribution.

## Learn text features from training only {.smaller}

**Vocabulary learned before the split**

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[All text] --> B[Learn word weights]
  B --> C[Split]
  C --> D[Fit and test]
```

**Vocabulary learned from training only**

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[Split] --> B[Learn words and model]
  B --> C[Apply to validation]
```

The first order lets validation or test words influence what the model keeps.

## A pipeline keeps the order together {.smaller}

A scikit-learn **pipeline** is one object that learns the text conversion and
the classifier in the correct order.

```python
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

def make_model(min_df):
    return make_pipeline(
        TfidfVectorizer(min_df=min_df),
        LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000),
    )

model = make_model(min_df=2)
model.fit(training["text"], training["label"])
prediction = model.predict(validation["text"])
```

`min_df` stands for **minimum document frequency**. Here, one document is one
request, so `min_df=2` keeps a word only if it appears in at least two training
requests.

## Validation chooses; test evaluates {.smaller}

```python
candidate_values = [1, 2, 5]
validation_scores = []

for value in candidate_values:
    model = make_model(min_df=value)
    model.fit(training["text"], training["label"])
    prediction = model.predict(validation["text"])
    validation_scores.append(accuracy_score(validation["label"], prediction))

selected_value = candidate_values[np.argmax(validation_scores)]
assert selected_value in candidate_values
```

The candidate list should be fixed before the scores are known. After choosing,
we refit the selected plan and open the test set once.

## “Open once” is a workflow rule {.smaller}

Before test evaluation, save:

- the rows assigned to each set;
- the allowed settings and tie-breaking rule;
- the main metric;
- the two comparisons;
- the practical threshold;
- the code checks that must pass.

After test evaluation, do not quietly revise these choices. New questions may
be studied, but they need to be labeled as follow-up work with new evidence.

## Read a difference and its interval together {.smaller}

Suppose the simple model is 71% accurate and the baseline is 40%
accurate on the same test cases.

$$
\text{observed improvement}=71\%-40\%=31\text{ percentage points}.
$$

If an uncertainty interval for the improvement is 21 to 40 points:

- the observed difference is 31 points;
- the whole interval is above zero;
- the simple model passes the signal check in this evaluation;
- the result still applies only to the cases the test set can represent.

An interval cannot compensate for a poor split or missing kinds of cases.

## Why the comparison is paired {.smaller}

For each test case, record whether each method is correct:

```{python}
#| echo: true
simple_correct   = np.array([1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1])
baseline_correct = np.array([1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1])

case_difference = simple_correct - baseline_correct
observed_difference = case_difference.mean()
observed_difference
```

Both methods predict the same cases, so we resample whole cases and keep the
two outcomes together. This is a **paired bootstrap**. It mimics drawing a new
set of cases while preserving the comparison within each case.

## Keep a record of the design decisions {.smaller .compact-table}

| What EDA or the study question reveals | Design decision | What to record |
|---|---|---|
| The target is later requests | split in time order | requests by year and set |
| Templates or people appear repeatedly | keep each group in one set | number of groups shared across sets |
| Vocabulary is a learned feature | learn it from training only | pipeline settings and training vocabulary |
| Test feedback could influence selection | choose on validation; evaluate test once | frozen choices and final test output |

A useful record says what changed, why it changed, and what evidence shows that
the final analysis followed the decision. “Leakage addressed” does not say
enough.

## EDA cannot create observations we do not have {.smaller}

After every design change, ask:

> Which kinds of requests are absent from the observed data?

Examples:

- only public text is available;
- short or sensitive requests were removed;
- only requests with one staff-assigned queue remain;
- the teaching sample contains selected categories in fixed numbers.

No split, model, or uncertainty interval can establish performance for cases
that were never observed. Narrow the target population or collect data from
the missing cases.

## Stronger AI prompts are stronger study plans {.smaller}

**Weak request**

> Determine whether the language model is better.

**Specified request**

> Compare the language model with the fixed simple model on the locked later
> test set. Use accuracy, report the paired difference and interval, and do not
> change categories or settings after seeing test results. State that the tool
> only recommends a queue for staff review.

The second prompt improves the analysis because it supplies missing decisions,
not because it sounds more polished.

## Two AI answers are a comparison, not an experiment {.smaller}

If a detailed prompt produces a better plan than a weak prompt, we may describe
the differences in those two answers.

We cannot conclude that every difference was caused by the prompt because AI
systems can vary from one response to another.

A stronger test of the prompt effect would use:

- many fresh conversations for each prompt;
- the same model and settings;
- a rule for scoring plan quality;
- a comparison of the two distributions of scores.

For Homework 3, the goal is careful auditing—not a full prompt experiment.

## Keep a short AI-use record {.smaller}

Record enough for another person to understand the workflow:

| Item | Example |
|---|---|
| Tool | name and version, when available |
| Purpose | draft a simulation or analysis plan |
| Initial prompt | exact request that began the work |
| Output used | code scaffold, explanation, or plan |
| Checks | fixed seed, overlap check, assertions, rerun |
| Human decision | split, metric, threshold, final claim |

The record shows what was delegated and what was verified.

## Keep this map beside the homework {.smaller}

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[Problem 1<br/>design in words] --> B[Problem 2<br/>use EDA and run code]
  B --> C[Problem 3<br/>compare AI plans]
```

- **Problem 1:** define the label, cases described, comparisons, split, and claim.
- **Problem 2:** document each design choice with EDA, code, or output, then
  open the test once.
- **Problem 3:** check whether a detailed prompt produces a more usable plan
  and retain responsibility for the final decisions.

The same five questions from Lecture A apply to all three problems.
